# Kaṇhajātaka (Ja 440)

**ID:** Ja 440
**Section:** Jātaka (ja)
**Collection:** Suttas-Late-1
**Title (Pali):** Kaṇhajātaka
**Title (English, SuttaCentral):** The Black Sage
**SuttaCentral:** https://suttacentral.net/ja440
**tipitaka.org (CST):** https://tipitaka.org/romn/cscd/s0513m.mul9.xml

## AI-generated Overview (from reference literature and SuttaCentral)

*This overview was drafted by an AI model from the cited scholarship and SuttaCentral data and may contain errors; verify against the sources before relying on it.*

The *Kaṇhajātaka* (Ja 440, PTS Jātaka IV 6ff.) is a canonical Pali birth story set in the Banyan Park (Nigrodhārāma) at Kapilavatthu [SuttaCentral; Lamotte]. According to the traditional frame story, the Buddha smiled while walking past a tree where the ascetic Kaṇha had practiced austerities—a tree that perpetually bore fruit by decree of the god Sakka—which prompted Ānanda to ask the reason for his smile [Lamotte; SuttaCentral]. In the story of the past, the Bodhisatta was born with a dark complexion and was given the name Kaṇha ("black") [Salomon 2018]. He took up the life of an ascetic and was tested by Sakka (Śakra), who provoked him with a verse repeating the word *kaṇha* three times in reference to both his skin and name; satisfied with Kaṇha's steadfast virtue and endurance, Sakka granted him boons, which the ascetic chose wisely [Hazra 1994; Salomon 2018]. The story is also referenced in later Pali literature, specifically in the *Milindapañha* (Mil 7.4.2, *Āpaṅgapañha*) [SuttaCentral].

Cross-textual and manuscript evidence links the verse tradition of the *Kaṇhajātaka* to other Indian narrative cycles. Notably, an early Gāndhārī manuscript containing the Viśvantara/Sudaṣṇa story cites a verse that directly matches the verse in the Pali *Kaṇhajātaka* rather than the *Vessantarajātaka*, reflecting thematic affinities between the two narratives regarding renunciation and testing by Śakra [Salomon 2018]. Text-reuse algorithms in DharmaNexus identify extensive Pali-internal connections, especially with the commentary *Jātaka-aṭṭhakathā* (51 matches), the *Akittijātaka* (Ja 480; 35 matches), the *Cariyāpiṭaka-aṭṭhakathā* (19 matches), the *Vessantarajātaka* (Ja 547; 12 matches), and the *Alambusājātaka* (Ja 523; 6 matches) [DharmaNexus]. DharmaNexus also aligns isolated lines with Sanskrit and Tibetan treatises and Mahāyāna sūtras, including Nāgārjuna's *Ratnāvalī* and the *Lalitavistara* [DharmaNexus]. Modern scholars have additionally cited the narrative to discuss structural features of the Jātaka genre [Collins 1998].
